title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview at the mint-Equitymaster Investor Hour on April 11, 2023
summary: A biographical interview covering Pabrai's childhood with a serially bankrupt entrepreneur father, his path from tech engineer to IT entrepreneur to fund manager, and the evolution of his strategy from Graham deep value to growth. He shares case studies (Satyam, Kotak, Blue Dart, IPSCO, Fiat Chrysler, the Turkish warehouse company, Coca-Cola Icecek vs Varun Beverages), his 'anomaly-based' investing philosophy, why selling should be extremely reluctant, how he handled inheritance for his daughters, and the Dakshana model.

ideas.idea: Highly levered businesses have no staying power when the first headwinds come — my father went bankrupt every three or four years.
ideas.detail: His father was brilliant at spotting offering gaps and starting businesses with zero money in 10 different industries, but took every rupee banks would lend and stepped on the gas, so businesses of 300-400 people blew up; the family had no money for rent or groceries in the busts.

ideas.idea: The window from age 11 to 20 is the only time in life when the brain is optimally set up to specialize, so start early.
ideas.detail: Bill Gates started programming at 11 and had 10-15,000 hours before 20; Buffett bought his first stock at 11; Pabrai got his own accidental business MBA by sitting as his father's 'board of directors' at 12 and going on sales calls at 16. Education systems force a jack-of-all-trades approach that wastes this window.

ideas.idea: You get good at a business when it is facing adversity, because that is when you turn over every rock.
ideas.detail: Each night he and his brother tried to figure out how to keep his father's collapsing business alive for one more day; his father learned the jewelry business from a stranger on a flight and exploited a UAE duty arbitrage that paid for Pabrai's US college.

ideas.idea: Buffett's 20-punch-card approach is night and day from a mutual fund with 100 stocks and 80% turnover — following Buffett should beat the professionals.
ideas.detail: After reading Peter Lynch's One Up On Wall Street and Beating The Street in 1994 he discovered Buffett; he tested the theory with $1 million in 10% bets starting in 1994 and turned it into $13 million in about five years, roughly 70% annualized.

ideas.idea: When one part of the market is frenzied, basic brick-and-mortar businesses get very cheap — do a complete 180 into Ben Graham deep value.
ideas.detail: The day Nasdaq peaked on March 9, 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low; funeral homes, steel mills and tankers traded at single-digit multiples and he bought a funeral home at 2x earnings. The fund was up 70% in its first year and did 37% a year before fees with no down years from 1999 to 2007.

ideas.idea: IPSCO was a classic Graham mathematical game: $15 of cash plus two years of $15 cash flow per share equals the $45 stock price, with the plants free.
ideas.detail: Bought in 2004 at $45, the stock drifted to $90 in under two years and a Swedish company then bid $160; he exited around $155 without waiting for the deal to close.

ideas.idea: I should have switched back from the Graham playbook to growth investing around 2012 — I was about eight years late.
ideas.detail: The best way to invest is usually to buy businesses that grow over time; the Graham playbook only made sense in extreme euphoria. Having run it comfortably for 13 years he didn't switch until around 2020, and even then carefully because 2022 valuations were crazy again.

ideas.idea: In 2007-09 the funds fell 65-67% versus 37% for the market; I was selling P/E of 3 to buy P/E of 2 and then made 140% in 2009.
ideas.detail: He did not see the financial crisis coming even after Michael Burry walked him through credit default swaps in his San Jose office in October 2008 — God took the horse to water but the horse didn't drink.

ideas.idea: Fiat Chrysler at a $5 billion market cap on $135 billion of revenue with a rock-star CEO was a huge multi-bagger.
ideas.detail: Bought in 2012 at under 4% of revenue; about $1.5 billion of the market cap was attributable to the 80% Ferrari stake, and Ferrari alone is now worth about $50 billion. Rain Industries in India was a similar multi-bagger.

ideas.idea: I don't spend any time on macro — figuring out one business is hard enough, and only a few humans can forecast an economy.
ideas.detail: He saw the 2000 bubble only because his 1998-99 private tech investments had already blown up; some bubbles like crypto or Snowflake are callable, but usually there is no clear signal. He also didn't understand COVID's severity, unlike Bill Ackman.

ideas.idea: Almost all businesses are very fragile — if a business loses revenue for a month, about 95% won't be around.
ideas.detail: Bill Gates built Microsoft's cash reserve to survive two years with no revenue, which 99% of businesses cannot do; Berkshire keeps its cash in short-term treasuries rather than any bank for the same reason and has for 50 years.

ideas.idea: Satyam in 1995 traded below the value of its Hyderabad real estate while growing 70-80% a year — it went from 40 rupees to 6,000, 150x.
ideas.detail: He put $10,000 of a $20,000 India allocation into Satyam through Kotak in 1994-95, sold in January 2000 for $1.4 million because the valuation could not be justified; the Kotak analyst's target was 55 rupees.

ideas.idea: When you own a fraction of a great business, just sit on your ass — selling Kotak and Blue Dart cost me 300-500x.
ideas.detail: He sold his flat-for-five-years Kotak and Blue Dart positions in 2000 to recover $10,000; Kotak went up ~500x and Blue Dart 300-400x. One 'fake' Blue Dart certificate of 100 shares he kept for 15 years sold for 8-9 lakhs.

ideas.idea: Rakesh Jhunjhunwala only had to get one thing right — buying Titan in 2003 and, more importantly, holding it.
ideas.detail: Jhunjhunwala started with $400 at 25 and died with $5.8 billion; his 4% position in Titan (about $3.4 million) grew to more than $2 billion with dividends. Investing is a very forgiving business.

ideas.idea: The best approach is anomaly-based investing: look for things that make no sense and pass unless you are astonished.
ideas.detail: Auction-driven markets throw up astonishing mispricings occasionally, not every year, but you only need one Titan, one Coke bottler, one Blue Dart.

ideas.idea: A Turkish warehouse company with a $16 million market cap and $760 million liquidation value is the kind of anomaly worth a third of the company.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: 12 million square feet, 99% leased on inflation-indexed leases to Ikea, Amazon, Carrefour, Mercedes, Toyota; at $80/sq ft replacement cost less $200 million debt. He bought one-third for under $8 million in 2019; market cap is now $350 million in dollars despite the lira going from 5 to 19 per dollar, and liquidation value is at least $1.5 billion. The only thing to do is never sell.

ideas.idea: Turkey is a gambling den where people buy at 10 and sell at 3 — the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: The Turkish market was up 120% in dollars last year yet remains one of the cheapest in the world with 80% inflation and no foreign interest; the high trading volume let him accumulate a position despite the tiny market cap.

ideas.idea: The Turkish Coke bottler trades at one-fourth the value of Varun Beverages while bottling almost three times the volume — an anomaly.
ideas.detail: Varun: ~$11 billion market cap, under 700 million cases, 50x trailing earnings; Coca-Cola Icecek: $2.8 billion market cap, 1.6 billion cases across a dozen countries, 9x trailing. Coca-Cola Atlanta sold 51% of the Pakistan bottler (400 million cases) to the Turkish company for $300 million, valuing it at $600 million, roughly 10% of Varun's valuation.

ideas.idea: Selling is harder than buying; be extremely reluctant to sell and only sell when the valuation is egregious, not merely overpriced.
ideas.detail: He has made more selling mistakes than buying mistakes. If a business earning $1 million bought for $8 million reaches $200 million, it should not have been sold at $30-50 million; past $100-150 million you can let it go. You can be sloppy and slow on selling — it's a great way to make your broker starve. Separate signal from noise: bad quarters are noise, but lost integrity, competitors eating their lunch, loss of low-cost position or secular decline are real signals.

ideas.idea: Stick to auction-driven stock markets because they are the only asset class that gets depressed and euphoric enough to create mispricings.
ideas.detail: A Mumbai flat appraised daily varies between 6 and 7 crores in a year, but inside a listed company it would trade between 3 and 9; private equity faces an intelligent seller and gets an intelligent price. The Turkish owners would have laughed at $25 million for the whole business, yet 30% was available in the market at that price. Gold and whole businesses don't offer this.

ideas.idea: A 100x trailing P/E on a software company is a signal of very high growth — better than buying the stock was starting a service practice around it.
ideas.detail: In the 1990s he launched a PeopleSoft practice for a $1,000 ad, hired Paul Yates at $250,000, and had $3,000/day billing plus 12 developers at $2,000/day before Yates even started; he repeated this with Business Objects. Be an inch wide and a mile deep.

ideas.idea: Give children a meaningful sum at 18 with full control so they choose careers by passion, not pay, and tell them nothing more is coming.
ideas.detail: Cloned from Bill Harlow, who put $6 million into Goldman accounts for his kids at 18; Pabrai funded UGMA accounts at $20-30,000 a year invested in 3-4 stocks, now seven figures each. Parents have 18 years to transfer values — without values the money is a problem, with values it is a huge positive.

ideas.idea: Reading must be fun; all knowledge is cumulative and business biographies are the best genre.
ideas.detail: More than half the books in his library are unread; a book must draw him in within 10-20 pages. The Munjal/Hero Honda biography taught him bicycles are not low-tech and that Honda chose the Munjals over the Tatas for their family values. He will never retire — he could have stopped working at 33 but it would have been a useless life.

ideas.idea: Dakshana spends about $3,000 per bright poor kid to get a 60-80% IIT admit rate versus 1.4% overall, leveraging 30-40x in government subsidy.
ideas.detail: Started in 2007 when he was 42, designed as a 'tuition bill' of 2% of net worth per year to learn giving early; families earning under 6-7,000 rupees a month see kids start at 5-10 lakhs, some now earning over $500,000. The government spends about 1.25 crore per IIT student, so Dakshana redirects that subsidy from the middle class to the poor.

ideas.idea: Compounding is driven by three factors — starting capital, rate of return and runway — and a long runway alone makes a monthly SIP into an index fund astonishing.
ideas.detail: You don't need to be a stock picker or find an advisor; just buy a midcap or small-cap index early, keep a savings rate and let the eighth wonder of the world work.
